MUQATIL:81:15-29/r1.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:81:15-29/r1.speaker: author
MUQATIL:81:15-29/r1.claim: When night darkens, its darkness covers every animal, including beetles, snakes, scorpions, predators, and wild beasts.

FARRA:v3p242/r2.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v3p242/r2.speaker: المفسرون
FARRA:v3p242/r2.claim: The commentators agree that ʿasʿasa here means that night has departed.

FARRA:v3p242/r3.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v3p242/r3.speaker: بعض أصحابنا
FARRA:v3p242/r3.claim: Some colleagues instead say ʿasʿasa means night approached its beginning and grew dark.

FARRA:v3p242/r4.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v3p242/r4.speaker: أبو البلاد النحوي
FARRA:v3p242/r4.claim: Abū al-Bilād cites a line using ʿasʿasa for approaching; al-Farrāʾ says they regarded the line as fabricated.

ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p352#2/r1.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Ṣanʿānī
ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p352#2/r1.speaker: قتادة
ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p352#2/r1.claim: Qatada says عسعس means that night has departed.

ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p352#2/r2.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Ṣanʿānī
ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p352#2/r2.speaker: الحسن
ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p352#2/r2.claim: Hasan says the night has covered the people.

ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p352#2/r3.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Ṣanʿānī
ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p352#2/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p352#2/r3.claim: Ibn Abbas says عسعس means that night has arrived.

TAB-FULL:v24p160/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p160/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v24p160/r1.claim: God swears by the night as it withdraws; Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatāda, and al-Ḍaḥḥāk also interpret it as departing.

TAB-FULL:v24p160/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p160/r2.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب
TAB-FULL:v24p160/r2.claim: Reports say ʿAlī recited the paired oath of night and dawn after dawn appeared, then said it was the time for Witr prayer.

TAB-FULL:v24p160/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p160/r3.speaker: مجاهد
TAB-FULL:v24p160/r3.claim: Mujāhid gives both senses for ʿasʿasa: the night coming on and its departure.

TAB-FULL:v24p161/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p161/r1.speaker: ابن زيد
TAB-FULL:v24p161/r1.claim: Ibn Zayd glosses ʿasʿasa as turning away, with dawn's breath beginning from the direction of sunrise.

TAB-FULL:v24p161/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p161/r2.speaker: الحسن
TAB-FULL:v24p161/r2.claim: Al-Ḥasan says the night covers people; ʿAṭiyya gestures toward the west for the night coming on.

TAB-FULL:v24p161/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p161/r3.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v24p161/r3.claim: Al-Ṭabarī prefers the night withdrawing because dawn is arriving; Arabic uses both ʿasʿasa and saʿsaʿa for a night nearing its end, as shown by poems of Ruʾba and ʿAlqama.

TAB-FULL:v24p161/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p161/r4.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v24p161/r4.claim: Some Arabic specialists say ʿasʿasa means night beginning and darkening, citing a line al-Farrāʾ says was likely fabricated.

ZAJJAJ:v5p291/r3.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v5p291/r3.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v5p291/r3.claim: Asʿasa can mean that night approaches or departs; both meanings relate to the beginning of darkness, at its onset or when it recedes at the end.

IBNABIHATIM:v10p3405#2/r1.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3405#2/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3405#2/r1.claim: Ibn Abbas glosses the night as receding and the dawn as the day beginning at the break of dawn.

NAHHAS:v5p159/r12.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v5p159/r12.speaker: الفراء
NAHHAS:v5p159/r12.claim: The wāw coordinates with the khunnas, not a new oath; al-Farrāʾ says exegetes agree ʿasʿasa means night approaching.

NAHHAS:v5p159/r13.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v5p159/r13.speaker: مجاهد
NAHHAS:v5p159/r13.claim: Mujāhid reports Ibn ʿAbbās interpreting ʿasʿasa as the night departing, against al-Farrāʾ.

THALABI:v10p141/r5.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p141/r5.speaker: الحسن
THALABI:v10p141/r5.claim: Hasan says ʿasʿasa means that night comes on with darkness.

THALABI:v10p141/r6.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p141/r6.speaker: author
THALABI:v10p141/r6.claim: Other authorities take ʿasʿasa as night withdrawing until little remains; Arabic usage and lines by Alqama and Ru'ba support this sense.

THALABI:v10p141/r7.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p141/r7.speaker: author
THALABI:v10p141/r7.claim: Alqama ibn Fart's line describes night withdrawing as dawn breathes.

THALABI:v10p141/r8.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p141/r8.speaker: author
THALABI:v10p141/r8.claim: Ru'ba's line likewise uses tasasʿa for night receding.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p217/r1.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p217/r1.speaker: ابن عباس وابن زيد
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p217/r1.claim: The night when it withdraws means when it has departed.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p217/r2.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p217/r2.speaker: ابن جبير وقتادة
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p217/r2.claim: It may mean when the night approaches; the root ʿass conveys fullness, describing night as it begins to fill or reaches full darkness.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p217/r3.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p217/r3.speaker: الشاعر
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p217/r3.claim: A cited line uses تنفس for the dawn's appearing as night clears away.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:81:18-20/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:81:18-20/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:81:18-20/r1.claim: For the neighboring oath, one view says night “when it darkens” means its arrival; another says its departure.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p349/r10.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p349/r10.speaker: الحسن
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p349/r10.claim: Al-Hasan says عسعس means night approached with darkness; others say it departed.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p349/r11.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p349/r11.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p349/r11.claim: Both عسعس and سعسع are Arabic for night’s departure, with little of it remaining.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p42#2/r1.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p42#2/r1.speaker: ابن عباس وابن زيد والفراء
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p42#2/r1.claim: One interpretation of ʿasʿasa is that night departs.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p42#2/r2.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p42#2/r2.speaker: ابن جبير وقتادة
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p42#2/r2.claim: Another interpretation is that night arrives.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p42#2/r3.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p42#2/r3.speaker: الزجاج
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p42#2/r3.claim: The verb is used for night either arriving or departing; those who understand it as departing cite the following oath by dawn.

RAZI-FULL:v31p66#3/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v31p66#3/r3.speaker: أهل اللغة
RAZI-FULL:v31p66#3/r3.claim: Arabic lexicographers say asʿasa is a contronym: the night may be said to asʿasa when it begins or when it ends.

RAZI-FULL:v31p66#3/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v31p66#3/r4.speaker: العجاج
RAZI-FULL:v31p66#3/r4.claim: Al-Ajjaj's verse uses asʿasa for night retreating as dawn breathes and the night departs.

RAZI-FULL:v31p66#3/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v31p66#3/r5.speaker: أبو عبيدة
RAZI-FULL:v31p66#3/r5.claim: Abu Ubayda cites a line using asʿasa for night arriving.

RAZI-FULL:v31p67/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v31p67/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v31p67/r1.claim: Some take asʿasa as the night coming on, paired with dawn's arrival; others take it as night retreating at the first light, followed by dawn becoming fully bright, like 74:33-34.

QURTUBI-FULL:81:15-22/r10.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:81:15-22/r10.speaker: الحسن
QURTUBI-FULL:81:15-22/r10.claim: An alternative report from Hasan and others says the night came on with its darkness.

QURTUBI-FULL:81:15-22/r11.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:81:15-22/r11.speaker: زيد بن أسلم
QURTUBI-FULL:81:15-22/r11.claim: He glosses ʿasʿasa simply as going away.

QURTUBI-FULL:81:15-22/r12.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:81:15-22/r12.speaker: الفراء
QURTUBI-FULL:81:15-22/r12.claim: Arabic speakers use ʿasʿasa or saʿsʿa when only a little of something remains.

QURTUBI-FULL:81:15-22/r13.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:81:15-22/r13.speaker: الخليل وغيره
QURTUBI-FULL:81:15-22/r13.claim: They say the night may either begin or end by ʿasʿasa.

QURTUBI-FULL:81:15-22/r14.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:81:15-22/r14.speaker: المبرد
QURTUBI-FULL:81:15-22/r14.claim: He calls it a word of opposite senses, which converge on darkness beginning at dusk and withdrawing at dawn.

QURTUBI-FULL:81:15-22/r15.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:81:15-22/r15.speaker: علقمة بن قرط
QURTUBI-FULL:81:15-22/r15.claim: His poem says the night departed as morning breathed, supporting the departing sense.

QURTUBI-FULL:81:15-22/r16.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:81:15-22/r16.speaker: رؤبة
QURTUBI-FULL:81:15-22/r16.claim: His poem uses saʿsaʿa for the night swiftly moving on, evidence cited for al-Farra's interpretation.

QURTUBI-FULL:81:15-22/r17.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:81:15-22/r17.speaker: امرؤ القيس
QURTUBI-FULL:81:15-22/r17.claim: His poem says the night approached close enough for a firebrand to be obtained, supporting the approaching sense.

QURTUBI-FULL:81:15-22/r18.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:81:15-22/r18.speaker: الحسن ومجاهد
QURTUBI-FULL:81:15-22/r18.claim: They also interpret ʿasʿasa as growing dark, supported by a poem about riding into deep darkness.

QURTUBI-FULL:81:15-22/r19.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:81:15-22/r19.speaker: الماوردي
QURTUBI-FULL:81:15-22/r19.claim: The root ʿas means fullness; night can begin filling with darkness or depart after becoming completely filled.

QURTUBI-FULL:81:15-22/r20.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:81:15-22/r20.speaker: امرؤ القيس
QURTUBI-FULL:81:15-22/r20.claim: In another line, ʿAsʿas is a place in the desert, not the verb describing night.

QURTUBI-FULL:81:15-22/r21.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:81:15-22/r21.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:81:15-22/r21.claim: ʿAsʿas is also a male name, used in a rajaz line.

QURTUBI-FULL:81:15-22/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:81:15-22/r7.speaker: الفراء
QURTUBI-FULL:81:15-22/r7.claim: Al-Farra says the commentators agree that ʿasʿasa means the night departed; al-Jawhari transmits this view.

QURTUBI-FULL:81:15-22/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:81:15-22/r8.speaker: بعض أصحابنا
QURTUBI-FULL:81:15-22/r8.claim: Some say the night approached at its beginning and grew dark, as clouds do when descending near the earth.

QURTUBI-FULL:81:15-22/r9.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:81:15-22/r9.speaker: ابن عباس ومجاهد
QURTUBI-FULL:81:15-22/r9.claim: They interpret the night as departing with its darkness.

BAYDAWI-FULL:81:15-21/r2.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:81:15-21/r2.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:81:15-21/r2.claim: عسعس is an opposite, meaning the night either approaches in darkness or withdraws.

NASAFI-FULL:v4p320#5/r1.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v4p320#5/r1.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v4p320#5/r1.claim: ʿAsʿasa is a word with opposite senses: night may be arriving in darkness or departing.

QASHANI:81:10-17/r6.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:81:10-17/r6.speaker: author
QASHANI:81:10-17/r6.claim: Night is the darkness of the dead body, beginning to recede as life-light appears when the soul attaches and its sun rises.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p412/r11.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p412/r11.speaker: الفراء
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p412/r11.claim: Al-Farraʾ says ʿasʿasa describes night when only a little of it remains.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p412/r12.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p412/r12.speaker: الخليل
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p412/r12.claim: Al-Khalil says ʿasʿasa can mean that night either approaches or departs.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p412/r13.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p412/r13.speaker: المبرد
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p412/r13.claim: Al-Mubarrad classifies ʿasʿasa as a word with opposite meanings.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p418/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p418/r4.speaker: الحسن
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p418/r4.claim: Al-Hasan takes ʿasʿasa as nightfall; its pairing with dawn, which breathes, supports two contrasting states.

SAMIN-DURR:81:17/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:81:17/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:81:17/r1.claim: ‘As‘asa’ and ‘sa‘sa‘a’ can mean to approach; in al-‘Ajjaj’s verse the dawn breathes, night clears away, and the night recedes.

SAMIN-DURR:81:17/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:81:17/r2.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:81:17/r2.claim: The verb may share both opposite senses, or specifically mean to recede in Quraysh usage.

SAMIN-DURR:81:17/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:81:17/r3.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:81:17/r3.claim: Another view says the darkness is arriving; its contrast with ‘when dawn breathes’ supports this sense, which is close to the night’s recession.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p337#2/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p337#2/r1.speaker: مجاهد
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p337#2/r1.claim: Mujahid glosses عسعس as darkness setting in, while other early authorities take it as night beginning or covering people.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p337#2/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p337#2/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p337#2/r2.claim: Ibn Abbas and several authorities understand عسعس as night departing; Mujahid is reported with both onset and departure readings.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p337#2/r3.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p337#2/r3.speaker: علي
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p337#2/r3.claim: Ali says the dawn prayer time is when night has withdrawn, in response to a question about the odd prayer and these paired oaths.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p337#2/r4.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p337#2/r4.speaker: ابن جرير
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p337#2/r4.claim: Ibn Jarir prefers night's retreat, pairing it with the dawn's becoming bright and citing a poet's line about dawn breathing and night departing.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p337#2/r5.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p337#2/r5.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p337#2/r5.claim: Ibn Kathir prefers night beginning, since its darkness pairs more fittingly with the dawn's first light; he links the image with other night-and-day oaths.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p337#2/r6.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p337#2/r6.speaker: علماء الأصول
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p337#2/r6.claim: Many legal theorists say عسعس is a shared term for night beginning and departing, so both senses can be intended.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p337#2/r7.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p337#2/r7.speaker: الفراء
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p337#2/r7.claim: Al-Farra reports an Arab grammarian's gloss that عسعس neared its beginning and darkened, but says the supporting verse was considered fabricated.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p335#s081/r1.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p335#s081/r1.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p335#s081/r1.claim: Al-Takwīr threatens the climactic Day of Judgment and chastises Qur’an deniers; the Qur’an is a reminder in honored, pure pages delivered by trusted angels.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p335/r1.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p335/r1.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p335/r1.claim: Al-Takwīr threatens the Day of Judgment as the climactic display of divine majesty and warns those who reject the Qur’an, a reminder preserved in honored, pure pages by angelic scribes.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p340#2/r1.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p340#2/r1.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p340#2/r1.claim: The Qur’an’s ordering of judgments, rulings, and knowledge is beyond human capacity and miraculous, so denying it brings the denier complete disgrace.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p340#2/r12.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p340#2/r12.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p340#2/r12.claim: Night is the setting where stars emerge as its darkness gathers and deepens after disappearing in daylight.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p340/r1.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p340/r1.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p340/r1.claim: The cosmic signs in al-Takwīr precede the flight from relatives in ʿAbasa, so the opening of this surah signals the Hour and answers when it will come.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p340/r2.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p340/r2.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p340/r2.claim: After associating disgrace with the verse about humanity’s ingratitude, Biqāʿī says the gravest denial after shirk is rejecting the truth, especially the Qur’an.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p341/r1.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p341/r1.speaker: قيل
BIQAI-FULL:v8p341/r1.claim: Unattributed readings take ʿasʿasa to mean that night departs, darkens, reaches its midpoint, or ends; the cognate verb also carries the sense.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p341/r2.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p341/r2.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p341/r2.claim: The rhetorical ellipsis mentions the stars’ retreat and concealment to imply their appearance, then mentions night to imply the omitted day.

DURR-FULL:v8p433/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p433/r2.speaker: مجاهد
DURR-FULL:v8p433/r2.claim: Mujahid says ʿasʿasa can mean the night arriving or departing.

DURR-FULL:v8p433/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p433/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v8p433/r3.claim: Ibn Abbas tells Nafi ibn al-Azraq that ʿasʿasa means the onset of darkness and cites al-Nabigha's poetry as evidence.

BURSEVI:v10p271/r6.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p271/r6.speaker: الوسيط
BURSEVI:v10p271/r6.claim: Al-Wasit takes asʿasa as night departing, since dawn rises as night withdraws and the order of mention follows their sequence in time.

BURSEVI:v10p271/r7.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p271/r7.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v10p271/r7.claim: Asʿasa can also mean night arriving, one of the root’s opposite meanings; Bursevi finds this better matched to the paired dawn clause.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p58#2/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p58#2/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
ALUSI-FULL:v30p58#2/r1.claim: Ibn Abbas and others are reported to explain ʿasʿasa as either the night drawing its darkness away or its darkness arriving.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p58#2/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p58#2/r2.speaker: المبرد
ALUSI-FULL:v30p58#2/r2.claim: Al-Mubarrad treats ʿasʿasa as a word with opposite meanings, while al-Raghib instead calls it a shared meaning: the thinness of darkness at both ends of night, not true antonymy.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p58#2/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p58#2/r3.speaker: الراغب
ALUSI-FULL:v30p58#2/r3.claim: Al-Raghib says the word denotes thin darkness at both the beginning and end of night, so its uses are related rather than opposite; he explains the verse with both arriving and departing.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p58#2/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p58#2/r4.speaker: الفراء
ALUSI-FULL:v30p58#2/r4.claim: Al-Farra says the exegetes agree that ʿasʿasa means that night departs, and cites al-ʿAjjāj's verse describing night as it ends.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p58#2/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p58#2/r5.speaker: العجاج
ALUSI-FULL:v30p58#2/r5.claim: Al-ʿAjjāj's line about wine or a desert witnesses night ending as dawn begins to breathe.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p58#2/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p58#2/r6.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p58#2/r6.claim: Some call this a specifically Qurashī usage; others say reading it as nightfall best fits the following reference to dawn.

ELMALILI:81:17-29#2/r1.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:81:17-29#2/r1.speaker: author
ELMALILI:81:17-29#2/r1.claim: As‘asa has opposite senses: the night’s approach and its departure, so the oath’s wording can carry either meaning.

ELMALILI:81:17-29#2/r2.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:81:17-29#2/r2.speaker: bazıları
ELMALILI:81:17-29#2/r2.claim: Some take the night’s approach as its first hours, when it begins to darken, which carries a warning.

ELMALILI:81:17-29#2/r3.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:81:17-29#2/r3.speaker: Ekseriyet
ELMALILI:81:17-29#2/r3.claim: Most commentators prefer the night’s departure, its final hours as it turns toward dawn, heralding the morning.

ELMALILI:81:17-29#2/r4.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:81:17-29#2/r4.speaker: Buhârî
ELMALILI:81:17-29#2/r4.claim: Bukhari also transmits the departing sense of as‘asa, making the phrase like the oath in 74:33; Elmalılı’s rendering is intended to suggest both senses.

ELMALILI:81:17-29#2/r6.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:81:17-29#2/r6.speaker: author
ELMALILI:81:17-29#2/r6.claim: The dawn dispels the distress of night and promises the Prophet and Muslims a good outcome, as expressed in 93:4.

ELMALILI:81:17-29#2/r7.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:81:17-29#2/r7.speaker: author
ELMALILI:81:17-29#2/r7.claim: The believers’ present world is a night turning toward morning, and the Judgment when each soul learns what it prepared is like a breathing dawn.

TABATABAI:81:15-18/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:81:15-18/r5.speaker: الراغب
TABATABAI:81:15-18/r5.claim: Raghib says ʿasʿasa can mean the night approaching or retreating, referring to twilight at either edge of night; the link with dawn favors its retreat here.

TABATABAI:81:15-18/r6.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:81:15-18/r6.speaker: قيل
TABATABAI:81:15-18/r6.claim: A view takes ʿasʿasa as the onset of night, but the author finds this distant in context.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p194/r3.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p194/r3.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p194/r3.claim: The stars and the night-to-dawn transition testify that the Qur'an is not soothsayer chant but was brought by God's mighty, honored, obeyed, trustworthy angel.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p201/r3.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p201/r3.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p201/r3.claim: The oath passage refutes the disbelievers' claim that neither the Qur'an is revelation nor Muhammad is God's messenger; they spread this charge to blunt the Prophet's influence.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p202/r1.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p202/r1.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p202/r1.claim: Soothsayers claimed contact with jinn who disclosed the unseen, casting their rhymed utterances as revelation; the Qur'an rejects the idea that the Prophet is their kind.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p203/r3.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p203/r3.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p203/r3.claim: The prefixed lā in these oaths is not denial of the oath; it negates the addressees' claim being refuted by the oath.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p205/r4.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p205/r4.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p205/r4.claim: The retreating night and breathing dawn form another oath that supports the preceding claim about the Qur'an.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p205/r5.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p205/r5.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p205/r5.claim: ʿAsʿas can mean either grow dark or withdraw and pass away; the author prefers the second sense, supported by the parallel wording at 74:33–34.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p206/r1.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p206/r1.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p206/r1.claim: The paired oaths substantiate the Hereafter as the premise under discussion.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:81:15/r1.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:81:15/r1.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:81:15/r1.claim: The elegant oaths in verses 15–18 confirm the coming claims about revelation and the Prophet and prepare listeners to grasp their importance; doubters would accept no religious message otherwise.

STUDYQURAN:81:17/r1.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:81:17/r1.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:81:17/r1.claim: ʿAsʿasa can mean either approach or leave, referring to the beginning or end of night, or both.

STUDYQURAN:81:18/r2.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:81:18/r2.speaker: some
STUDYQURAN:81:18/r2.claim: If night approaches in verse 17, this verse refers to morning rising; if night recedes, it refers to morning's rise or gradual illumination.
